stakeholders.name: protestant_reformers
stakeholders.situation: Theological dissidents who gained a distribution channel for vernacular scripture and doctrinal texts that bypassed ecclesiastical gatekeepers. The press allowed them to reach audiences at scale and speed impossible under manuscript production, transforming localized dissent into continent-wide movements. They commissioned translations, wrote pamphlets, and coordinated printer networks.

stakeholders.name: commercial_printers
stakeholders.situation: Entrepreneurs who discovered vernacular religious texts were a profitable market segment. They invested in type, paper, and distribution networks to serve demand for Bibles, catechisms, and polemics in local languages. Their commercial incentive aligned with reformers' theological goals, creating a self-sustaining production system.

stakeholders.name: literate_laity
stakeholders.situation: Gained direct access to scriptural texts in languages they could read, reducing dependence on clerical interpretation. The availability of printed vernacular Bibles allowed independent engagement with religious authority claims, though literacy rates and book costs still constrained access for many.

stakeholders.name: catholic_church_hierarchy
stakeholders.situation: Lost monopoly control over scriptural interpretation and religious text distribution. The institutional structure had relied on Latin texts, clerical mediation, and manuscript scarcity to maintain doctrinal authority. The press made suppression of heterodox texts logistically infeasible at scale, forcing reactive measures like the Index Librorum Prohibitorum.

stakeholders.name: manuscript_scriptoria
stakeholders.situation: Monastic and commercial manuscript production centers whose economic model collapsed as printed books undercut their cost structure by orders of magnitude. Scribal labor could not compete with mechanical reproduction; most scriptoria closed or converted to other functions within a generation.

stakeholders.name: technology_historians
stakeholders.situation: Analyze whether the Reformation was caused by printing technology or whether reformers and printers exploited an available technology for their own purposes. They examine adoption rates, censorship attempts, and counterfactual scenarios to assess the causal structure.

six_questions.coordination_function: The printing press solved the technical problem of text reproduction at scale: movable type allowed rapid, accurate, low-cost duplication of written material, making information goods accessible beyond manuscript economics.
six_questions.transfer_function: Transferred control over religious text distribution from ecclesiastical institutions to a distributed network of printers, translators, and readers. Shifted revenue from manuscript production to commercial printing. Transferred interpretive authority from clergy to literate laity with direct textual access.
six_questions.absent_voices: Illiterate populations who could not read vernacular texts even when available, and whose religious practice remained mediated by oral tradition and clerical authority regardless of printing technology. Their exclusion from the literacy-dependent benefits is structurally invisible in the technological-inevitability framing.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: Technological determinists argue vernacular scripture spread was inevitable once printing existed—the technology made suppression impossible and the Reformation unavoidable. Beneficiary-focused historians argue the spread required active coordination by reformers and printers who chose to produce and distribute vernacular texts despite censorship risk, and that the technology alone did not determine its use. The constraint's classification turns on this causal dispute.
six_questions.founding_problem: Pre-printing manuscript production created a bottleneck: religious texts were scarce, expensive, controlled by institutions, and available only in Latin to most of Europe. Vernacular access required either rare translated manuscripts or clerical mediation.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Technology historians and book-history scholars from outside the reformer or printer beneficiary groups confirm the scarcity problem was solved by printing technology within decades of Gutenberg. The constraint's persistence as a framing device (technological inevitability) is what remains contested, not the original production bottleneck.

commentary.narrative_context:
The printing press enabled mass production of vernacular scripture in 16th-century Europe, breaking the Catholic Church's monopoly on religious text distribution. This constraint story examines whether vernacular scripture spread was a natural consequence of printing technology (mountain) or a coordinated effort by reformers and printers who benefited from the disruption (false summit). The claimed type is mountain, reflecting the technological-determinism framing. The metrics describe moderate extraction rising over time as the inevitability narrative became entrenched, with declining suppression as censorship became logistically infeasible.

KEY AGENTS (by structural relationship):
- Protestant reformers: Primary beneficiary (organized/mobile) — gained distribution channel bypassing ecclesiastical control
- Commercial printers: Primary beneficiary (moderate/mobile) — discovered profitable market in vernacular religious texts
- Literate laity: Secondary beneficiary (moderate/constrained) — gained direct scriptural access
- Catholic Church hierarchy: Primary target (institutional/constrained) — lost interpretive monopoly and text control
- Manuscript scriptoria: Secondary target (moderate/trapped) — economic model collapsed under printing competition
- Technology historians: Analytical observer — examines causal structure of technology vs. agency
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness starts low (0.15) when printing is a neutral technology and rises to moderate (0.42) as the inevitability framing becomes historiographically entrenched, benefiting those who profit from technological-determinism narratives. Suppression starts moderate-high (0.45) reflecting initial censorship attempts and declines (0.28) as the scale of printing made suppression logistically impossible—this is genuine technological constraint, not enforcement decay. Theater ratio is low throughout (0.05 to 0.18) because the printing technology itself functions as claimed; the theatrical element is the inevitability framing layered over genuine technical capability. Accessibility collapse is substantial (0.72) because once printing exists and vernacular texts circulate, manuscript-based control becomes structurally unviable. Resistance is moderate (0.35) because the Church mounted real suppression efforts (Index, censorship, printer persecution) even as the technology made those efforts increasingly futile.
commentary.directionality_logic: Protestant reformers and commercial printers are structural beneficiaries with mobile exit options—they chose to use printing for vernacular texts and could have chosen otherwise. The Church hierarchy is the primary target with constrained exit—the institution's authority structure depended on text control that printing technology undermined. Literate laity are beneficiaries but with constrained exit because literacy and book costs still limited access. Manuscript scriptoria are trapped targets whose livelihood was destroyed by technological substitution. The analytical observer seat examines the causal structure without stake in the outcome.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the reformer and printer seats, the constraint appears as a coordination opportunity they actively exploited—printing was a tool they wielded for theological and commercial goals. From the Church hierarchy seat, the constraint appears as an external technological force that made their prior control structure obsolete regardless of their response. From the analytical seat, the question is whether the technology determined the outcome or whether human agency shaped how the technology was deployed. The engine should compute different types across these seats based on their structural positions.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The mountain claim (technological inevitability) must be distinguished from the coordination claim (reformers and printers chose to produce vernacular texts). A genuine mountain would show near-zero extraction and resistance; the moderate values here suggest identifiable beneficiaries shaped the outcome. The false-summit machinery should flag this: a mountain with declared beneficiaries whose extraction rises over time as the inevitability narrative becomes entrenched. The founding problem (manuscript scarcity) is genuinely solved, but the constraint's persistence as a historiographic framing device serves the beneficiaries' interests.

omegas.question: Was vernacular scripture spread an inevitable consequence of printing technology, or did it require active coordination by reformers and printers who chose to produce and distribute such texts despite censorship risk?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Comparative analysis of printing adoption in regions with and without organized reform movements; examination of printers' choices about what to print; counterfactual analysis of whether printing alone, absent reformer demand and coordination, would have produced the same outcome.
omegas.impact: If inevitable, the constraint is a genuine mountain (technological law). If agency-dependent, it is a false summit—a coordination mechanism benefiting reformers and printers, framed as natural law to obscure the beneficiary structure.
omegas.description: Whether the constraint is natural law or constructed coordination.

omegas.question: How much of the measured extraction comes from the literacy barrier that excluded most of the population from the technology's benefits, versus extraction from the inevitability framing itself?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Historical literacy rate data; analysis of who could actually access printed vernacular texts; examination of oral-tradition religious practice that continued unchanged despite printing.
omegas.impact: If most extraction comes from literacy barriers, the constraint's extractiveness is a function of education access, not printing technology. If extraction comes from the framing, it is historiographic rent-seeking by technological determinists.
omegas.description: Source of measured extraction: structural literacy barriers vs. framing benefits.

omegas.question: At what point did the scale of printing make censorship logistically impossible versus merely difficult? Was there a window where suppression could have succeeded with sufficient institutional commitment?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Analysis of censorship success rates over time; examination of regions where suppression was more effective; assessment of the Church's resource allocation to censorship efforts.
omegas.impact: If censorship became impossible early, the declining suppression metric reflects genuine technological constraint (mountain-supporting). If a window existed where greater effort could have succeeded, the Church's failure to suppress reflects institutional choice or resource constraints, not technological inevitability (false-summit-supporting).
omegas.description: Whether censorship futility was technologically determined or institutionally contingent.

network.dual_formulation_note: This constraint is presented as a single historical phenomenon (printing caused the Reformation) but decomposes into at least two distinct claims: (1) printing technology made text reproduction cheap and scalable (genuine mountain—physics and economics of movable type), and (2) vernacular scripture spread was inevitable once printing existed (contested—requires beneficiary coordination to explain why printers chose religious texts over other content, why reformers organized translation and distribution, and why the Church's suppression failed). The ε values differ substantially: the technology constraint has negligible extraction; the inevitability framing has moderate extraction rising over time. This story models the composite claim as currently framed in popular historiography; a full decomposition would separate the technology constraint from the agency-dependent diffusion pattern.
